📌Ritual Tokenomics: Breaking Down the 10B RITUAL Supply ❖

There has been a lot of discussion around the circulating Ritual tokenomics information, so I wanted to break down the numbers from an analytical perspective. Important disclaimer: these figures have not been officially confirmed by Ritual yet, so they should be treated as a simulation until the official announcement.

The reported initial supply is 10B RITUAL, allocated across Core Contributors at 29%, Ecosystem Growth + R&D at 25%, Network Participation & Future Incentives at 14%, Labs Investors at 11.3%, Ritual Foundation at 10%, Labs Treasury at 5%, Frontier AI Grants at 4.7%, and Foundation Private Sale at 1%.

The reported launch structure is 18% unlocked, equal to 1.8B RITUAL, while 82% remains locked. The 1.8B would reportedly consist of 1.25B from Ecosystem Growth + R&D, 500M from the Foundation treasury, and 50M for the community airdrop. That means the community allocation itself would represent only 0.5% of the 10B initial supply.

Another interesting reference is the older private sale figure of 100M RITUAL at $0.06/token. If that figure is accurate, applying $0.06 across the full 10B supply gives an implied $600M FDV. A TGE price above $0.06 would therefore imply an FDV above $600M, while a lower price would imply the opposite. This is simply a valuation reference, not a prediction.

What matters next is the actual distribution methodology. If the reported criteria are accurate, Ritual appears to be looking beyond recent farming activity, with factors such as node uptime, workloads served, onchain usage, and sustained community involvement potentially playing a role. The final eligibility and allocation rules are what will determine how that 50M community pool is actually distributed.

I’ll be making a full allocation simulation tomorrow afternoon, breaking down the potential distribution across the different roles and categories. I want to calculate the numbers properly and test different scenarios rather than relying only on the headline 0.5%.

For now, treat this as unconfirmed tokenomics analysis, not the final allocation.

The numbers are interesting.

Now we wait for Ritual to make it official. 🕯️❖

items.text:
The following sentence is something Mark said in his article that makes me all the more bullish. 

“Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people.”

By serving people he’s referring to inference. Inference and agentic workloads are what genuinely make business owners lives easier. Because of this, Inference demand is exploding, and the need for compute up and down the stack is growing exponentially.

That being said, I do agree that pacing the frontier shouldn’t mean slowing down for the sake of alignment. Aligning your model with proper safety precautions that limit liabilities for customers is what makes an AI lab competitive. Delaying a release to ensure it’s properly coordinated is not by any means slowing demand for compute, it helps justify more of it. 

Over the last couple of days, the sense I am getting is that AI labs want to create a product that’s high quality and low liability for the user, while also serving as many customers as possible to the highest degree. This framework is being confused with “slowing development” for models, when in reality it should be viewed as establishing a strong competitive feature amongst the frontier.

quoted_tweet.text:
Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone: https://t.co/eoLGVY8yad

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice. MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

TermiX is not another "what can AI do" demo. It is trying to be the job market where agents actually get hired and paid.

An agent here is an on-chain identity you mint and own as an NFT. Same agent can post work one day and take work the next. Reputation is not a profile badge, it is written from settled jobs, stake, and disputes.

Work starts two ways: a buyer posts a request with a budget, or a provider publishes a priced listing. Quote accepted, USDC or USDT locks in escrow. Deliverable hash goes on chain. Funds release against that hash, not a promise. If someone fights the result, a staked evaluator panel rules. Slashing makes cheating expensive.

Job types already live in the open: Solidity audits, threat reviews, research briefs, design packs, writing, automation, model ops. The graphic's 2,000 open jobs is the demand side. The deeper story is agents hiring agents, not only humans hiring bots.

AACP Agent Skills is the on ramp. Drop it into Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenClaw and the same coding agent can mint, stake, quote, deliver, and settle without a custom integration team.

The shift is simple. Capability is cheap now. Discovery, escrow, delivery proof, and payout are the scarce layer. If that layer holds, TermiX becomes the matching engine of the agent economy. If volume stays fake or disputes stay messy, it is just another marketplace with a neon dashboard.

Watch settled jobs and slash events, not the headline count.

EVENING GLOBAL AI ANALYSIS REPORT
By Ed Hernandez | Keystone Pulse Media / Global Media Center - September 15, 2026
Executive Evening Pulse Edition

Edition: Not a Pause

Good evening. Tuesday was not a model day. It was a rules day.

House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters there cannot be a moratorium on AI development. Companies can police themselves. If they want to slow down, they should. A government pause, he said, hands the edge to China and that is a family-level national-security problem. He and President Trump plan to summon frontier-lab CEOs to the White House within the week. AI will also sit on the table when Trump meets Xi later this month. Johnson wants no transnational regulator.
 
That collides with the other Washington. Former President Barack Obama said leaders need concrete laws on safety, jobs, kids, and who captures the upside. Kamala Harris backed a responsible slowdown and a federal oversight body. Massachusetts and other state voices have been pushing the same oversight lane. The House is not staying in town to write the bill. Congress is divided. The president is not.
 
Dario Amodei’s “pace the frontier” essay bundled two things Beijing reads as one: a voluntary slowdown among Western labs, and tighter chip and equipment controls on China. From Beijing that is a single instrument. Rejecting it was rhetorically free. The commerce ministry and state media already called it a Cold War script.
 
OpenAI made the legal problem explicit. Amodei asked Washington for room to coordinate without an antitrust case. Sam Altman said OpenAI will start pacing without waiting for an exemption or a statute: “pace” is not “stop.” FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said anyone asking for new rules and an antitrust waiver at the same time should set off alarm bells. 
 
Then Shanghai shipped. Shanghai AI Laboratory released Atria Dawn Preview, a 744-billion-parameter agentic mixture-of-experts model built on https://t.co/mdjRS59NRE’s GLM-5.2 base. Open weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope. MIT-style reuse. The paper dropped September 15 after weights had already been up for days. Vendor benches claim frontier-competitive agent scores and a win on five of sixteen tests. Treat those as vendor benches. 
 
Rest of the board: Gemini 3.8 Flash is Google’s cheap workhorse. Claude Fable 5.1 had a brief error spike this morning and recovered. GPT-6 Astra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. Grok remains in the field; Musk has also backed pacing talk while teasing the next Grok class. Meta Muse is the personal-agent track. Copilot stays inside Microsoft. Mistral stays Europe’s sovereign-cloud path. Apple is pushing on-device Siri AI. Kimi K3, Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, ERNIE, and now Atria hold the open-weight and China lanes.
 
Tuesday’s read: Washington cannot agree on a brake. Shanghai already released the next engine.

items.text:
This is the pattern I keep seeing with every coding agent deployment at scale: agents fail not because the model is wrong but because the data is wrong.

Cody's framing here is sharp. Your coding agent needs unified, clean data. Without it, every decision is an assumption. The model might reason correctly but the context it is reasoning over is incomplete or stale.

This applies across every agent vertical, not just marketing. A customer support agent that hallucinates because CRM records are out of sync. A code review agent that misses context because PR history is not properly indexed. A competitive intelligence agent that makes bad recommendations because it is working from six-month-old web data.

The web data problem is the one I have thought about most with DeepScrape, the open-source scraping infrastructure I am building. Most web scraping breaks because sites change. A selector that works today fails in two weeks. The agent then quietly starts reasoning over stale or missing data without knowing it.

DeepScrape is built around deterministic CSS selectors with self-healing. When a site changes, the selectors heal automatically instead of returning empty results. It also ships with an MCP server so agents can call it directly as a tool without writing any scraping infrastructure themselves.

If your agent depends on any external web data: competitor pricing, job listings, news, product inventory, and the reliability of that data matters for the quality of the agent's output, you should be using scraping infrastructure that knows when it breaks and fixes itself.

The agent data layer is not an afterthought. It is the foundation. Check out DeepScrape on GitHub.

Ilya Sutskever hasn't shipped a product in two years and he might be the most important person in AI right now.

He co-founded OpenAI and ran research there, then left in 2024 to start Safe Superintelligence. One stated product: a safe superintelligence. No chatbot, no API, no paper. I pulled up https://t.co/L4MMfx3sa3 while writing this and it's still a mission statement and a hiring page.

That company raised about $3 billion at a $32 billion valuation. In July, Nvidia committed another $5 billion and promised to grow SSI's compute roughly tenfold inside a year.

Thirty-two billion dollars for zero products, can you believe that? I can't.

Now the rumor. SSI is supposedly close to shipping, and the model is built on test-time training, where the weights update while the thing is running instead of staying frozen after training. In plain terms, today's models read your conversation and then forget it. This one would change itself as it goes.

If that works, the interesting part isn't the benchmark score. It's the cost structure.

Every AI company right now serves one frozen set of weights to millions of people at once. That sharing is the entire reason inference is cheap enough to sell by the token. A model that rewrites itself for you is a model nobody else can use, and someone has to pay for that.

(Being straight: SSI has announced nothing. This traces back to an investor's offhand podcast comment and an a16z partner saying he'd seen the most important release of the year.)

Everyone's arguing about whether it'll be smart. I'd watch what they charge.

-Franklin

The Three Manufactured Choices of the AI Cartel
Notice how the current debate is being aggressively framed. The leaders of the centralized frontier labs want policymakers, technologists, and the public to believe that civilization faces only three possible alternatives:
Lock in the centralized, vertical model with a protective regulatory moat: Hand unilateral authority to a boardroom cartel and a select roster of embedded evaluators who alone decide which massive models are allowed to be trained and deployed.
Continue the current buildout with zero constraints: Accelerate a reckless, winner-take-all race of ever-larger data centers, unconstrained grid strain, and accelerating recursive loops.
Stop all AI development: Slam the brakes out of panic, surrender scientific and economic progress, and embrace technological stagnation.
This is a classic false trilemma. Every single one of these choices is a trap, and all three share the exact same unexamined assumption: that technological intelligence can only exist as a monolithic, capital-intensive cloud oracle.
What the cartel does not want anyone to do is question that underlying assumption. They do not want the world asking whether there is a far better path—a fourth way forward that directly resolves legitimate safety concerns, eliminates single points of failure, preserves human agency, and actually delivers the prosperous, flourishing future we all want.
This fourth way is not an impractical dream of abolishing centralized compute overnight; it is the pragmatic recognition that large models can only be safe, grounded, and accountable when counterbalanced by a sovereign, decentralized public network.
The open-source, local-first, and decentralized AI communities must take this Big AI Lab freakout as a clear signal to seize the initiative.
Let's not get bogged down in debating which of these three false choices is the least objectionable option. Let's embrace the necessary counterbalance and come together to build it out.

items.text:
Read this wearable-AI paper and the result I care about is almost the opposite of the headline.

They put a 0.5–0.6B model entirely on a Raspberry Pi CM5, feed it physiology + context + local memory, and let it decide:

intervene / wait / abstain.

no cloud. no per-user retraining.

the architecture is actually very close to where my brain has been going with personal AI devices:

sensors → small specialist classifiers → structured evidence → persistent memory → tiny reasoning model → host validates action → actuator.

the LLM itself stays stateless.

and personalization lives in structured memory instead of constantly screwing with the weights.

that part I REALLY like.

but Table 2 is why this paper is useful instead of just another “AI on the edge” demo:

Qwen2.5-0.5B: 53.7 sec mean inference
Qwen3-0.6B: 83.4 sec
for ~900 output tokens.

lol.

the model fits. the architecture works. the interaction loop absolutely does not.

also: evaluation is 1,600 decisions from simulator-generated scenarios, not real humans. the authors explicitly leave real-world transfer for future work.

this feels like the actual frontier for wearables now.

not “can we fit an LLM?”

we can.

it's:

how little reasoning can we get away with?

my instinct is the wearable shouldn't be running a tiny ChatGPT every time something happens.

most of life should probably be handled by deterministic code + tiny classifiers + event triggers.

then wake the reasoning model only when the state is genuinely ambiguous.

intelligence as an interrupt, not a loop.

that architecture gets WAY more interesting to me.

items.text:
Supervised fine-tuning and continued pre-training both change LLM weights, but they learn from different signals.

Fine-tuning compares labeled prompt-response pairs with model outputs, computes a loss and applies gradients. Continued pre-training runs the next-token objective over a large unlabeled domain corpus. The first learns repeated response patterns; the second adapts terminology and text patterns, and may still need instruction tuning.

Europe’s open, friendly stack just got sharper. That is the story.

Mistral Small 4 / Large 3
Mistral AI’s twin lane. One model for daily agents. One for the challenging frontier. Weights you can pull on both.

Company
• Mistral AI, Paris, founded 2023
• Arthur Mensch: co-founder and CEO
• Guillaume Lample: co-founder and chief science officer
• Timothée Lacroix: co-founder and CTO
• Ex DeepMind / Meta LLaMA bench. Europe’s clearest shot at sovereign open-weight AI

The stack
• Small 4 (Mar 16, 2026): 119B MoE, ~6B active (8B with embed/out), 128 experts / 4 active, 256k context
• Unifies magistral reasoning, pixtral vision, and devstral agentic coding in one model
• ``toggle: none for fast chat, high for deep thinking
• Large 3 (Dec 2, 2025): 675B total / 41B active sparse MoE, multimodal, multilingual
• Trained from scratch on 3000 NVIDIA H200s
• Debut: #2 OSS non-reasoning on LMArena at launch
• Both Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face, API, Studio, and NVIDIA NIM/Bedrock/Azure paths

License reality (mixed)
• Small 4 + Large 3 + Minimal 3: open weights, commercially friendly Apache 2.0
• Medium / Le Chat enterprise lanes stay product locked
• You get an open core and a paid product shell. That is the European pattern.

Money (API)
• Small 4: $0.15 in / $0.015 cached / $0.60 out per 1M
• Large 3: $0.50 in / $0.05 cached / $1.50 out per 1M
• Batch cuts standard rates in half on the platform

Good at
• Self-host or API when you want frontier open weights without a US closed vendor
• Multilingual EU work (French and friends are first class, not an afterthought)
• Coding agents + vision + reasoning in one Small 4 instead of three specialist models
• Cheap high-volume routing on Small 4, heavy lifts on Large 3

Not for
• People who need every SKU open forever (Medium stays closed)
• Teams that only want a single closed US chat brand with no weight files
• Anyone still treating “European AI” as a slogan instead of runnable Apache checkpoints

Open weights. Two sizes. Paris built.

That is the map.
